extracted.intended_audience: readers and learners of natural philosophy/early‑modern experimental science (students, amateur experimenters, educated lay readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and experimental demonstrations in hydrostatics (laws of fluid pressure, buoyancy, lateral pressure) and elementary chymical (chemical) operations with acids and alkalies, intended to show phenomena and infer general laws. Includes step‑by‑step experiment descriptions, proportions, and explanatory reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate action of solids from fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: If we rightly distinguish the Action of Solid from that of Fluid Bodies, this Objection will fall itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sand‑bank (solid) vs liquid vessel thought‑experiment: a body just below the sand surface bears far less pressure than one deeply buried in sand, but in a liquid the same relative positions experience equal pressure according to the law of pressure. The point is to evaluate whether a medium transmits pressure like a solid (depends on quantity/surface) or like a fluid (depends on depth alone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of pressure in fluids (pressure depends on depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: All Liquids which have others on the side of them, do exert a real Force, which presses upwards ... the Law of Pressure in fluid Matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that pressure at a point in a fluid depends on the vertical depth (height of fluid column) and is transmitted in all directions. Use experiments comparing bodies at the same horizontal plane under fluid versus under solid granular material to show the fluid law. Note the contrast: in fluids pressure is governed strictly by depth (height), not by the total quantity or breadth of fluid above a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and perform the lead/tin‑tube buoyancy experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment of Mr. Boyle: take a tin tube whose lower orifice is smooth, place a round piece of lead (thickness ~ a small fraction of an inch) over the mouth, fix a small hook and string through the lead, draw it tight, then let down suddenly into a large vessel of water with depth about 13–14 times the thickness of the lead; upon loosening the string the lead will be supported and swim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the described apparatus: smooth lower orifice, lead piece fitted to stop the orifice, a small hook near the middle, string tied. Depth matters: when the lead is placed ~13–14 times deeper than its own thickness it is supported by upward pressure; if placed only ~10–11 times its thickness it will sink. The experiment demonstrates upward fluid pressure supporting a denser object when the surrounding column of water provides greater upward pressure than the object's downward weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain buoyancy via comparative columns and density ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning: if the lead is about twelve times as heavy as the like quantity of water, but is placed beneath a water column thirteen times its thickness, the water underneath presses upwards with thirteen parts while the lead presses downwards with only twelve, so the lead must emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining buoyancy, compare the weight (density) of the object to the weight of an imagined vertical column of fluid of the same cross‑section and height equal to the object's submerged thickness. Use numeric ratios (as in the text: lead ~12× water; column ~13× thickness) to show when upward pressure exceeds downward weight. This is the expected explanatory pattern for similar demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate lateral pressure depends only on depth (dyke example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lateral pressure of fluids is regulated by depth; a dyke bears no greater burden than the pressure of the little water of equal height, not of the whole sea pressing at that side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the dyke/sea figure: show that even if the whole sea presses against a dyke, the force the dyke must resist equals that due to the depth (height) of water adjacent to it (a column of height equal to the sea level), not the total volume or breadth of the sea. This is the operative principle for designing and reasoning about retaining walls/dykes—test by comparing pressures at equal depths regardless of horizontal extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the pressure‑law to justify ships' flotation and navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Piece of Wood, and much more the smallest Ship, would sink like a Stone to the Bottom, if it were not kept floating by the Pressure of the Water upwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating designs or phenomena of floating bodies, invoke the upward pressure of fluids as the mechanism preventing sinking. Demonstrations and calculations should show how the upward pressure on submerged surfaces supports the vessel's weight; absence of this law would make navigation impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show effervescence when mixing acids and alkalies
rubrics_metrics.description: The famous Effects produced by Acids and Alcalies: put beaten Crabs‑Eyes (an alkali) into Vinegar (an acid) and you will presently see effects; mixing iron filings with spirit of saltpetre produces more violent motion and heat; mixing spirit of sal ammoniac with potash and an acid spirit shows strong effervescence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To demonstrate chemical action between acids and alkalies, use small, observable mixtures (crab's eyes + vinegar for mild action; iron filings + spirit of saltpetre for violent action). Expect effervescence, heat, and gas evolution. These are standard, repeatable classroom/home experiments to illustrate reactivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe formation of new salts and loss of original properties
rubrics_metrics.description: After these motions both the Acids and Alcalies lose their former properties ... being closely united to each other, do thereby produce a third Constitution entirely different from each of the former (called Salſum, Enixum, Muriaticum, Neutrum or Mixtum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record that mixtures of acids and alkalies often produce new salts with different taste and properties. Note changes such as loss of sharpness or volatility. Identify and name the resulting salts where appropriate, and use taste/volatility/effervescence as qualitative indicators (with modern safety caveat: do not taste hazardous substances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate precipitation and displacement among acid/alkali salts
rubrics_metrics.description: When some Alcalies and Acids are united and 'saturated' they may not act on others; yet there are laws by which one acid or alkali can displace another, separating previously united pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use displacement trials: e.g., pour spirit of sea‑salt (an acid) upon the alcaline salt of tartar and observe effervescence and union; then add water and spirit of saltpetre to cause the sea‑salt acid to quit its alkali and be replaced by saltpetre, producing burning saltpetre which can be further treated. Similar displacements occur among alcalies (adding a second alkali can free the first from its acid). These procedures illustrate relative affinities and separation techniques in qualitative chemistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use addition of water/other acids to separate tightly‑bound salts
rubrics_metrics.description: What is hard to separate by mere heat can be made to 'quit' an alkali by the addition of water and another acid (example: acid spirit of sea‑salt leaves its alkali when water and spirit of saltpetre are added).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to separate a strongly bound acid‑alkali product, try introducing a third reagent (another acid or water) that will form a more volatile or separable compound with one component, allowing extraction by gentle heat from sand or by other means. The text gives stepwise examples for saltpetre/tartar/seasalt sequences as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize acids and alcalies are widespread in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Acids are found in animals (milk, serum), minerals (sulphur, copperas, salt‑petre), plants (many fruits), medicinals springs, and the air (which corrodes iron). Alcaline salts likewise occur in animal parts (volatile salts), burnt shells, hartshorn, many plants and mineral waters, and even soot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing natural substances or preparing experiments, consider that acidic and alkaline materials are common across biological, vegetal, mineral, and atmospheric sources. Use distillation, calcination, or extraction (ashes, lixivial salts) to obtain such salts for demonstration. Consult cited natural‑history sources if necessary for local examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiments as evidence for general natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: From the foregoing experiments and observations (hydrostatics and chemical operations) one may conclude there are laws by which particles move or rest, and these regularities support broader inferences about order in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame experiments (hydrostatic and chymical) not only to show phenomena but to test and support general propositions: e.g., that particles obey regular laws, that pressure in fluids behaves according to depth, that acids/alkalies have predictable interactions. Present results with reasoned explanations comparing observed motions/changes to hypothesised laws.
